questions: If elected, what is your vision for improved transportation in North Vancouver?
Costs are rising and small business is feeling the squeeze. What will you do to support small businesses and foster business and job growth in North Vancouver?

answers.name: Dave Kurvers
answers.answer1: North Vancouver needs transportation that fits North Vancouver. I do not think the answer is simply more buses on already congested streets. Regional rapid transit and local North Shore movement are different problems. Regional rapid transit can terminate in North Vancouver, with passengers transferring into a local east-west network designed around North Shore destinations. That network could include privately developed urban ropeways providing frequent, grade-separated service. We also need to get our priorities right at street level. The City’s pre-pandemic 2019 North Shore Transportation Survey found that 19.6% of daily trips by City residents were on foot and 2.1% by bicycle. The sidewalk is our busiest active-transportation network and, on a commercial street, it is the critical connection between storefronts and customers. A bike lane is not automatically an improvement if it breaks that relationship or removes needed loading, deliveries, trades access and short-term customer access. Before changing a commercial street, the City should measure those impacts before and after. My goal is reliable local movement, strong regional connections and transportation infrastructure that supports neighbourhood life and local business.
answers.answer2: My approach is business retention before business attraction. Before chasing the next investment, City Hall should make sure the businesses already here can survive, expand and reinvest. A complete, straightforward business-licence application should receive a City decision within one week. Commercial permits should have published service standards, clear checklists, early zoning confirmation and one City contact coordinating the file. Where a new business takes over substantially the same lawful use, we should carry forward valid approvals and infrastructure wherever legally possible instead of starting from zero. City delay also has a real cost. Businesses can burn rent, wages and working capital while waiting for approvals. I would track City-controlled delay, repeat reviews and whether service standards are actually being met. I also want an annual Local Business Health Report, with quarterly permitting metrics, so Council can see openings, closures, vacancies and whether City decisions are helping or hurting commercial streets. Before changing parking, loading, vehicle access, curb space or streetscape design, the City should assess the business impact and measure the results afterward. A City that says it is open for business should be able to prove it.

answers.name: Linda Buchanan
answers.answer1: Moving safely and efficiently across the NS is a priority. It requires commitment from everyone from individuals, businesses and all levels of government. Together, over the last 4 years we have made progress but there is more work to do. Locally, my focus is on continuing to deliver the City’s Mobility Strategy (2022) - providing more choices for people to get where they are going, making it easier and safer for everyone to move around, and improving the reliable movement of people and goods. As more people come to the NS for employment and move through us to other destinations we feel the impacts. I will continue to work to segregate regional from local traffic, improve neighbourhood safety and traffic calming, and will deliver more work-force housing like at NSNH. Regionally, as Mayor, Chair of NS Connects, and a member of Translink Mayor’s Council, I will continue to be a strong advocate to senior governments for the replacement of Ironworkers Memorial Bridge and funding for full Bus Rapid Transit to the NS. There is no single solution - we need a connected transportation network that works for both people and the economy. That is my continued focus and commitment.
answers.answer2: A strong local economy requires partnership, leadership, and purposeful action. Our City is open for business, and small business is at its heart. I support a Team Canada approach that aligns local, provincial, and national priorities to strengthen our economy and respond to external pressures, as reflected in my 2025 Notice of Motion responding to U.S. Tariffs. My focus is on delivering the City’s Economic Strategy (2024): expanding economic opportunities, making it easier to do business, investing in vibrant public spaces, and building a resilient, future-focused economy. I will continue working directly with the Chamber, BIAs, and local businesses to understand cost pressures, reduce barriers, and ensure the business community has a strong voice in our annual budgeting process. Economic development also means investing in what businesses and workers need to succeed—housing, childcare, and better transportation options and I will continue to champion these. Looking ahead, I will advance the Great Streets Project and Health Innovation District, attract new investment including a new hotel, and leverage the opportunity to strengthen our port, shipbuilding, tech, and film industries. These investments will support local businesses, create jobs, attract investment, and foster a resilient local economy for the future.

answers.name: Andrew Robertson
answers.answer1: Big fixes like better crossings, highway upgrades, and rail transit will take lots of time and money. We must keep advocating for these while staying focused on what the City of North Vancouver can do now with our limited resources: make it easier to choose transit over driving with more reliable and frequent buses and dry, clean, well-lit stops; make it easier to bike or roll by completing a safe, connected mobility network; make it easier go without a parking spot and car ownership costs by expanding car shares; reduce bridge commuter numbers with workforce housing and growth near transit; and push the Province to fund bus rapid transit to Vancouver and Burnaby.
answers.answer2: Small businesses are the heart of North Vancouver and make areas like Lonsdale feel like home. The City can do a lot more to support them and the strong local economy they provide. That includes faster, simpler permitting, streets and public spaces that draw people in, and priority for local vendors at places like Shipyards events. It also means a legacy business retention program to help long-time shops stay open, and making sure the workers and customers local businesses rely on can afford to live locally and get around our city easily. I believe that workforce housing that supports North Vancouver’s workers’ ability to affordably live in the community they serve is an essential solution to our housing, affordability, and transportation crises that we must begin working on immediately. As a health innovator, I am also particularly excited by the potential of the proposed Health Innovation District as a new economic driver for Central Lonsdale.

answers.name: Angela Girard
answers.answer1: If elected, my vision is a City where people have real choices about how they get around: reliable transit, safe walking and cycling routes, and a road network that works for everyone. North Vancouver is a job-producing region, and it needs efficient, reliable movement of workers and goods. The biggest change available is rapid transit across the Inlet: a fixed, frequent connection on and off the North Shore. We're seeing what better regional transit can do. TransLink extended the R2 RapidBus to Metrotown, giving Park Royal a direct, all-day SkyTrain connection, delivered over three months early. I'll keep pressing senior governments and TransLink to invest, and keep working through North Shore Connects, uniting our three municipalities and two First Nations to advocate with one voice. Locally, we need to deliver the City's Mobility Strategy and make short trips easier by foot, bike or bus. I'll support an All Ages and Abilities bike network, including completing the Eastside Connector to Casano Drive, plus safer sidewalks, crossings, lighting and intersections. We can't build our way out of congestion, but we can offer better alternatives. The goal is simple: spend less of your life in a vehicle and more in our community.
answers.answer2: Small businesses need a City that recognizes rising costs and removes barriers, making it straightforward to operate and invest here. I will press to streamline licensing, planning and permitting so businesses get clear requirements and faster decisions. I will keep business property tax rates competitive with neighbouring municipalities and advocate for provincial property-tax changes that ease the burden on commercial tenants, since rising rents make it harder for independent businesses to open and stay. Now that paid parking is a reality, I will advocate for street signage explaining the parking app and clearer wayfinding to parkades, making it easier for customers to support local businesses. I will support the City's two BIAs, the growth of the brewery and health innovation districts, and the cultural precinct, given the economic benefits they bring. Finally, staff retention is a challenge, driven by limited affordable housing, childcare and transportation. On Council, I pushed to expand childcare on City lands, in new developments and at Cloverley School, where City funding is making it happen. I supported housing with mid-market rentals, including 89 affordable rentals at the North Shore Neighbourhood House. I will keep advocating for these so people can both work and live here.

answers.name: Anna Boltenko
answers.answer1: My vision is a North Vancouver where people, workers and goods can move reliably—not a city where everyone loses hours to congestion. Transportation is an economic issue. I will press for faster, more frequent and dependable transit; practical bus-priority measures; and sustained advocacy to TransLink and the Province for rapid transit connecting the North Shore to the regional network. The City must coordinate closely with the District, Squamish Nation and regional partners because congestion does not stop at municipal boundaries. Within the City, I will support safer, connected walking and cycling routes, accessible sidewalks, better links to transit and safer school zones. These choices give more people a realistic alternative to driving and free road capacity for trades, deliveries and those who must travel by car. Businesses also need dependable loading access, sensible curb management and better coordination of construction and roadwork. Finally, housing near jobs, services and transit must be part of the transportation solution. My approach is not cars versus bikes or buses. It is about moving more people efficiently, safely and predictably.
answers.answer2: As a nonprofit founder and active Chamber member, I understand that “support local” must mean more than a slogan. Small businesses need City Hall to be responsive, predictable and easy to navigate. I will push for a one-stop business navigator, clear service standards and published timelines for licences, permits and inspections. The City should review fees and processes with small-business owners, eliminate duplication and communicate changes before they create unexpected costs. We must protect employment lands and encourage flexible, appropriately sized commercial spaces so independent businesses, startups and service providers can remain here. City procurement should give local and Indigenous small businesses a fair opportunity to compete. Business growth also depends on workforce stability. More attainable housing, childcare and reliable transportation will help employers recruit and retain people. Vibrant streets, festivals, markets, patios and welcoming public spaces bring customers to local businesses. I will work with the Chamber, BIAs and entrepreneurs to implement the City’s Economic Strategy—with measurable targets, regular reporting and a simple test: is it becoming easier to start, operate and grow a business in North Vancouver?

answers.name: Don Bell
answers.answer1: Traffic congestion is a problem affecting movement of people and commercial traffic in North Van. We have road allowances created over 100 years ago with smaller populations. Improvements can be made to public transit, existing roads and signalization. Plan for increased growth of commercial truck delivery of goods and services to residents, local businesses and industry. We also must meet future needs for movement of employees, retail customers, medical visits, restaurant workers and customers, and commuters both to and from our community. Future options include making public transit more frequent, dependable , affordable and convenient, hopefully encouraging commuters who don’t need a car for their work to take transit. Include both vehicle and transit capacity in future improvements of the Iron Workers Memorial Bridge and possibly a North Shore version of Skytrain or new fast rail commuter service. The recently announced R2 Rapid Bus Park Royal to Metrotown is a step in the right direction. Providing truly affordable housing options would allow more business employees to live closer to their employment. The major options for improving transportation will require significant funding and co-operation from senior levels of government. North Van residents and businesses must be included in planning future transportation.
answers.answer2: Small and “Mom & Pop” retail businesses, medical, professional and technical offices, restaurants, pubs and coffee shops bring vitality of our local economy. Starting with the Covid Pandemic followed by economic uncertainty, both world- wide and locally, are challenges businesses have faced. Affordable housing options are needed for local workers to be able to live closer to their work and reduce the need for long distance commuting, especially if it involves crossing bridges to the North Shore. Public transit that is more frequent, dependable , affordable and convenient will help businesses attract and retain employees. Streamline City licencing and permit processes, and approval times to reduce costs that businesses require starting up or renovating. Enhancing the street level shopping experience by street trees, landscaping and street benches that allow shoppers to rest. Improvements to street customer parking, including better signage identifying nearby off-street public parking would help attract customers. Review with businesses possible improvements to the Pay Parking program, including the amount of free parking time. Review the residential to business tax ratios of the annual tax allocation compared to other similar communities. Protect our existing Light Industrial areas and their value to our economy.

answers.name: Jeremy Cato
answers.answer1: We have two traffic problems: how our own streets work, and a North Shore that still depends on two bridges built in 1938 and 1960. Locally, much is cheap to fix: a bad signal sequence, a confusing intersection, a Lonsdale traffic lane still taken up by a pandemic-era patio. I'd set up a public mobility task force: residents, business owners and City engineers working through the list together, with every decision explained publicly. Until a transit alternative exists, I'd keep full road capacity on the main routes to the bridges. Your staff, customers and deliveries depend on them. The bigger fix is rapid transit that doesn't sit in bridge traffic. In 2021, this Chamber and five North Shore governments commissioned a study finding roughly $600 million in benefits and 1,100 fewer crashes in 2050 alone. Employers told that study they lose job candidates once the commute is explained. Five years later, there's no price tag, no funding and no start date. In my first 90 days, I'll move a motion asking Ottawa to make North Shore rapid transit a project of national interest, with the City reporting publicly every year on results.
answers.answer2: Bruce Peters built Zazou from three chairs in 1992 to about 70 employees. He told me plainly: "It is getting more difficult to do business." He's not alone. The biggest cost increases, like payroll tax, minimum wage and sales tax, are set in Victoria and Ottawa. I'll be honest about that. But City Hall controls property taxes, permits, licences, curb rules and street design. Here's what I'd do with them. Hold the municipal property-tax increase at or below inflation, with a public explanation for any year it goes higher. Start with a full review of City spending, including sharing services with the District and West Vancouver, before anyone talks about cuts or new fees. Publish target times for permits and business licences, and report whether we meet them. Time is money. Set patio, loading and curb rules with the businesses affected, not after the fact. Grow the customer base. Redeveloping the soon-empty ICBC waterfront site into homes, jobs and a public destination, financed mainly by senior governments and private partners, would bring new residents, workers and visitors to Lower Lonsdale. And I'll press Victoria to raise the Employer Health Tax threshold for small employers.

answers.name: Jessica McIlroy
answers.answer1: It’s important for the city to address mobility in two separate ways, the movement of people and goods within the city, and the movement of people and goods on and off the North Shore. The existing mobility strategy has created actions that address safe and accessible transportation options for residents within the city, prioritizing active transportation, transit, and mode share. We need to continue implementing these actions to support a greater diversity of mobility options, improve pedestrian and cyclist safety, and decrease emissions while improving health outcomes. The major transportation issues and frustrations faced by North Vancouver residents relate mostly to movement on and off the North Shore. High traffic volumes and accidents cause bridge delays, leading to rat running through residential neighbourhoods and inefficient movement in the region. To address this larger issue, all North Shore governments must work together to ensure bus rapid transit is implemented while advocating to the province for a plan to replace the Ironworkers Memorial Bridge.
answers.answer2: The most important things within the city’s control to support local businesses are to streamline and simplify permitting processes, find ways to ease tax burdens such as through a development potential relief program or permitted tax exemptions, invest in regional improvements through plans such as the Great Street Project. The city can also create policies that define retail and commercial unit sizes in new buildings, to encourage smaller units for local retail and support medical and industrial spaces where needed. A more defined policy is needed on what type of businesses are preferred for streetscape spaces vs off-street and second or third floor spaces. The city can also advocate to the province for changes to property assessments, triple net leases, and to fund and reopen Small Business BC. There has been a long standing challenge with the assessment process using “highest and best use” calculations, which affects property taxes and how those costs are passed on to tenants. Given that over 90% of businesses in BC are small businesses, an organization that provides support services is needed.

answers.name: Jullian Kolstee
answers.answer1: Transportation should be safe, reliable, and accessible for residents and businesses, whatever the mode. Our major infrastructure and public transit are inadequate, but the city can only advocate along with the districts of North and West Vancouver to the province and Translink respectively. Bus Rapid Transit is what is available to us for now, and that requires transit priority in order to bypass congestion. Improving our active transportation network and streetscapes are tools that the city has to incentivize alternative modes of transportation, along with denser mixed-use communities that commuters can afford to live in. I’m most concerned with the resilience of our transportation infrastructure. We’re well aware of how disruptive a simple accident on one crossing can be, and that would be multiplied were a crossing to be compromised, or in the event of a major emergency on the North Shore. Escalating the need for resilient and redundant critical infrastructure from a transportation issue to an emergency management issue shifts the priority ahead, and I believe that is appropriate in our case.
answers.answer2: Our city should partner with small businesses as stakeholders in our community and local economy. These local businesses offer employment to residents, provide us with services, and are essential contributors to the city’s revenues. This means offering businesses clear processes to start and operate in the city, ensuring that streets and public spaces are attractive to customers, and that the city’s services meet their needs. Working with the city should be predictable for small businesses, easy to understand and navigate. The city’s economic development is tied to transportation infrastructure for goods, services, and labour, as well as affordability for workers to be able to live where they work, and for local patrons of small businesses. One metric I would use to judge our success is the longevity of businesses in the city. As a councillor I am looking for long-term partners in the business community who want to contribute to the future of our city.

answers.name: Ken Izatt
answers.answer1: As a retired business owner, I understand what it takes to run a viable business. Our transportation network needs immediate attention, starting with a collaborative review of our City’s 2022 Mobility Strategy to ensure our infrastructure keeps people and goods moving efficiently. At the same time, supporting small business must be a top municipal priority as it is the backbone of our local economy. Fostering job growth in North Vancouver requires targeted policies that reduce friction and lower overhead for local operators: • Streamline Permitting & Licensing: Fast-track commercial permits and implement a single-window digital portal to cut wait times for business openings and renovations. • Protect Commercial Space: Safeguard ground-floor retail and light industrial zones along key corridors like Lonsdale and Marine Drive against conversion into purely residential developments. • Cut Red Tape: Permanently simplify processes for patio, outdoor retail, and flexible space operations. • Support Local Innovation: Partner with local business associations and institutions to drive shop-local initiatives and worker retention. Building a resilient, local economy requires smart transportation and real support for business owners.

answers.name: Krishna Raisinghani
answers.answer1: Getting around should be easier and more reliable, whether you’re commuting to work, making deliveries, taking a child to school, or travelling across the North Shore. The new R2 connection to Metrotown is a welcome step, but we need to keep going. I’ll work with TransLink, neighbouring municipalities, and senior governments to improve transit frequency and reliability, strengthen connections across the North Shore and into the region, and advance the next generation of rapid transit. At the City level, I believe we can focus on short-term practical improvements: addressing bottlenecks and intersection issues using data and resident feedback, improving signal coordination, and closing gaps in safe walking and cycling routes. Transportation planning also has to work for businesses. That means considering employees, customers, deliveries, trades, and people with disabilities when we redesign streets or change how people move through the city. My goal is simple: give people more reliable choices and make it easier to move around North Vancouver.
answers.answer2: My parents ran a small store near Lonsdale and 15th, so I grew up seeing how much work goes into keeping a local business going. With costs rising, City Hall should make it easier to open, operate, and grow a business. I’ll bring a strong financial lens to the City budget and work to keep property tax and fee increases as low and predictable as reasonably possible. Businesses and residents deserve to know what is driving costs and what they’re getting in return. I’ll also push for clearer permit requirements and timelines, faster processing for straightforward applications, and one accountable City contact for complex files. Time spent waiting for approvals is a real cost for a business. A strong local economy also depends on access to workers. That means more housing choices, better transportation connections, and protecting space for local jobs and services. I want businesses involved earlier in City decisions. Supporting small businesses means listening, controlling the costs we can control, reducing unnecessary red tape, and creating better conditions to invest and grow.

answers.name: Max Lai
answers.answer1: If elected, I will ensure policies champion viable transportation options to both current and future needs. Policies include; • Advocating for implementation of a 25$ Low Income Transit Pass Program (Credit given to City of Vancouver Councilor Sean Orr) • Advocating for more than one BRT line such as BRT from Ambleside to Deep Cove, Upper Lonsdale to Burnaby via Highway 1 to other alternatives such as advocating to see the viability of implementing a street-car route through the Great Streets Project via Lonsdale Corridor • Continuation of NSTS, “North Shore Transportation Survey” to ensure clear and precise reporting on current, deliverable actions and anticipating future travel needs • Working with and advocating for Translink and senior levels of government to ensure robust North Shore Infrastructure Investment includes a replacement plan for our aging bridges as well as additional, rapid transit systems such as Skytrain or Light Rail • Updating the current Mobility Strategy through usage of NSTS to show clear, precise and accountable details of North Shore’s Transit Plan for the upcoming 4-8-12 years on building for and around our infrastructure issues
answers.answer2: Municipal government can help small businesses and foster business and job growth by; 1) Making access to and from the North Shore easier to get to and easier to leave when it comes to navigating the traffic gridlock. As seen with the above question, my vision for better transit on the North Shore is long-term and precise on what I want to achieve. 2) Decreasing current bureaucracy within City Hall itself. What this means is ensuring that interacting with City Hall is fast, efficient and reliable. We can do this by increasing speed for permits which will help increase the ease to start a business. We should make bylaws easier to read and understand, easing the obstacle of access to determine if certain requirements have been met to even cleaning up any processes in determining a permit to increase efficiency. 3) Advocating for the creation of a workforce housing program, securing 20% of net new units to be dedicated for individuals and families earning $30-80000 per year as the high cost of living on the North Shore is become more and more of a detriment for our young professionals and young families who wish to live and work here.

answers.name: Sean Alexander
answers.answer1: I respect Council’s democratically fostered mandate and aim to constructively build on our strengths. Good governance requires consulting experts, knowing we cannot solve this alone. Urban planners confirm we cannot simply build our way out of gridlock; that is like trying to lose weight by buying bigger pants. Crucially, driving remains non- negotiable for trades, delivery trucks, and service workers who power our local economy. Unaddressed gridlock acts as an invisible tax on small businesses, wasting billable hours and fuel. True fiscal responsibility means investing strategically to eliminate this economic drain. My vision deploys an agile transportation model: micro- shuttle networks and high-frequency feeder routes to solve the "last-mile" commute across key business corridors. Moving beyond temporary measures, I advocate for broad, continuous financial incentives for public transit. Shifted driving habits require cultural change, but making transit the most affordable, low-friction option across our four-year mandate will incentivize choice riders to leave their cars at home. Our goal is a tangible 10% to 15% traffic reduction this term. Achieving this shift lifts that invisible tax: clearing vital road space for commercial freight and services, recovering lost economic time, and improving quality of life across North Vancouver.
answers.answer2: Small businesses are the financial backbone and social engine of North Vancouver, yet recent municipal policies have left too many of them behind. In pursuit of ideal walkability targets, decisions made around streetscapes and parking, such as along East Esplanade and the St. Andrews corridor, have ignored practical business realities, with some local owners warning these changes are creating ghost towns. Governance cannot be driven by legacy projects or vanity goals that sacrifice local commerce. True representation means ensuring every business owner has a voice before decisions are finalized, and ensuring no corridor is left behind in the name of top-down planning. My platform restores active service and personal accountability to City Hall. I promise to listen, actively represent your concerns to Council, and stand available to answer for decisions when policies impact your livelihood. Through a guaranteed 48-hour response time and year-round corridor check-ins, I will work to influence Council with real economic feedback, ensuring City Hall serves local business, rather than pushing it aside.

answers.name: Shervin Shahriari
answers.answer1: We need to make inroads on transportation in North Vancouver. Businesses need employees, and many commute to and from the North Shore, often spending a long time in traffic. Congestion also affects the movement of goods and services. I support more frequent bus and SeaBus service, and I will push for full provincial funding for Bus Rapid Transit (BRT), which is currently being planned to run between Burnaby, North Vancouver, and West Vancouver. It is planned to be relatively fast, with traffic signal priority. We also need to improve traffic flow and safety, while ensuring new development provides adequate off-street parking. Pay parking has also frustrated some businesses, and we need to listen to their concerns and adjust as necessary. I support safe active transportation. One idea worth exploring is one-way streets in some areas, which could support active transportation and retain parking spaces. I would like to discuss ideas like this with the business community and residents, and get their feedback before moving forward. We should reduce bridge traffic by creating more housing for people who work here, so fewer workers need to commute across the bridges every day. This can also help with employee recruitment and retention.
answers.answer2: My focus would be on making it easier to do business with the City. City business services, including licensing and permitting, should be more streamlined. I support better lighting and regular maintenance to make our commercial streets more welcoming and attractive. Pedestrian safety is another priority for me, and I recently brought forward a successful motion to develop a phased pedestrian safety and e- mobility signage program, alongside education and enforcement efforts. I will emphasize financial stewardship and look for ways to minimize business property tax increases. I would also like to assess measures to provide tax relief to small businesses whose properties are assessed partly on their future development potential, rather than their current use. We should assess the impact of pay parking on small businesses and consider changes to its hours and its implementation to make it more convenient for evening customers, increase visits to many small retail and restaurant businesses, and make it easier for seniors to use, where technology is a barrier. Affordable housing for employees is also a priority for me. It can help with recruitment and retention. Shipyards programming brings businesses to Lower Lonsdale, and we need improved programming elsewhere, including in Central Lonsdale.

answers.name: Tammy Bentz
answers.answer1: North Vancouver doesn’t need another transportation plan that looks beautiful in a binder while everyone is stuck in traffic. We need a transportation system that actually works. My vision is simple: make it easier to get where you’re going—whether you’re walking, rolling, biking, taking the bus, or driving. That means safer, connected walking and cycling routes, better transit frequency and reliability, and serious advocacy for rapid transit across the North Shore. But being pro-transit doesn’t mean being anti-car. People still need vehicles— especially tradespeople, caregivers, families, people with disabilities and businesses moving goods. We should stop pretending that every transportation problem can be solved by adding another bike lane, or another lane for cars. I’d push for practical, data-driven decisions about how we use our limited street space, with priority for safety, transit, emergency response and essential deliveries. And I’d measure whether projects actually improve travel times and safety—not just whether we successfully spent the money. The goal? A North Vancouver where getting around is less of a daily endurance sport.
answers.answer2: Small businesses don’t need City Hall to “support” them by giving them another 47- page form to fill out. They need us to make it easier to open, operate and grow a business. I’d focus on three things: less bureaucracy, more affordability and better streets. The City’s own Economic Strategy calls for simpler licensing, coordinated services and better understanding of the cost pressures facing small businesses. I’d make those commitments real, measurable and accountable. That means a genuine one-stop business service at City Hall, faster and more predictable approvals, regular conversations with business owners, and a serious review of municipal fees, regulations and processes that add costs without adding value. We also need to make our commercial neighbourhoods places people want to visit—not merely places they drive through. Good public spaces, sensible parking and curb management, attractive main streets and support for local entrepreneurs can help create the foot traffic that small businesses depend on. And I want North Vancouver attracting good jobs and innovative businesses—not just more condos with a coffee shop at ground level. Economic development should mean more opportunity, not more paperwork.

answers.name: Tony Valente
answers.answer1: My vision for improved transportation is focused on one question: how do we move more people, more efficiently, through the limited road space we have? That starts with delivering the North Shore’s first major rapid transit option. If re- elected, I will continue to champion Bus Rapid Transit, with dedicated lanes, transit priority, frequent service and well-designed stations. BRT can provide a fast, reliable alternative to driving while making better use of the corridors we already have. We should also use new technology and smarter transportation systems to improve traffic flow, manage congestion and make transit more reliable. Longer term, I will continue advocating with regional and provincial partners for a new Second Narrows crossing. My approach is also about choice. Whether you walk, roll, cycle, drive or take transit, you should be able to move safely and efficiently. Before being elected, I chaired the HUB North Shore Committee, and on Council I have supported the City’s Mobility Strategy, protected mobility routes, RapidBus and expanded shared micromobility. Active transportation remains important, especially for shorter trips and connecting people to transit. The larger goal is a system that moves more people, not simply more vehicles.
answers.answer2: Small businesses are the backbone of North Vancouver’s economy, and if re- elected, I will continue supporting the conditions they need to succeed. A strong local economy depends on more than business policy alone. We need housing choices, transportation options, public spaces and amenities that allow people to live, work and spend time in our community. More housing helps employers attract and retain talent, allows more workers to live closer to their jobs, and brings customers within walking distance of local shops and services. Great public spaces are also economic infrastructure. The Shipyards has shown how thoughtful investment in the public realm can draw people into an area, increase foot traffic and create opportunities for restaurants, retailers and other businesses. As a founding member and director of the North Van Urban Forum, I helped bring residents together around the future of the waterfront and Shipyards district. I will also continue advocating for fairer property taxation, including for businesses affected by “highest and best use” assessments, support strong BIAs, and encourage commercial spaces in new developments that work for local businesses.

answers.name: Graham Alexander
answers.answer1: North Vancouver’s traffic gridlock is a daily economic drain that requires bold engineering action rather than status-quo tinkering. My vision is built on three pillars: First, we must aggressively pursue Skytrain expansion to the North Shore through an innovative private investment model to bypass regional transit bottlenecks and connect our community to the broader metropolitan network. Second, we will implement immediate, data-driven traffic management solutions on our municipal corridors—modernizing signal synchronization and adding 1,000 new parking spots to support local commerce and alleviate street congestion. Third, we will slash bureaucratic red tape and streamline infrastructure approvals, ensuring that road and transit upgrades are delivered efficiently without endless delays. By combining high-capacity rapid transit with smart traffic engineering, we will keep North Vancouver moving, reduce commute times, and connect residents to jobs and opportunities.
answers.answer2: Small businesses are being squeezed by rising operational costs, excessive municipal taxation, and administrative red tape. To foster business and job growth, City Hall must stop wasting taxpayer money and get out of the way of local enterprise. First, we must demand absolute fiscal accountability by conducting a forensic audit of municipal budget overruns—such as the North Shore Wastewater Treatment Plant escalation from $700 million to nearly $4 billion—to stop passing administrative waste and soaring property taxes onto small businesses. Second, we will slash red tape by implementing AI-powered instant building permits and streamlining municipal licensing. This eliminates costly construction delays and bureaucratic bottlenecks for local shops, restaurants, and startups. Finally, we will establish a predictable, pro-business regulatory environment that encourages commercial investment and rewards entrepreneurship. By eliminating wasteful municipal spending, lowering the tax burden, and modernizing licensing through technology, we will create a thriving, fair marketplace where North Vancouver businesses can hire, innovate, and flourish.

answers.name: Max Zahedi
answers.answer1: If elected, what is your vision for improved transportation in North Vancouver? I know traffic is one of the biggest concerns for businesses and all of North Shorain. People are tired of long commutes, buses stuck in the same traffic as cars, and neighbourhood streets filling up whenever the highway backs up. In my first 100 days, I would identify our ten worst bottlenecks, publish the list and get to work on practical fixes. That means better signal timing and coordinating road construction so one project does not make another traffic problem worse. I would work with TransLink and the Province on more reliable buses and bus priority where it makes sense. We also need safer crossings and better connections for people who walk or cycle. Housing and transportation have to be planned together. Building more homes near good transit gives people a real choice to drive less. During rush hour, I would work with the responsible agencies to position tow trucks near major trouble spots so disabled vehicles can be cleared sooner. I would also explore traffic cameras on the crossing that could help responders assess collisions and reopen roads safely, with clear privacy protections. I want people to spend less time stuck in traffic and more time living their lives.
answers.answer2: Costs are rising and small business is feeling the squeeze. What will you do to support small businesses and foster business and job growth in North Vancouver? My wife and I own a small dental clinic in Edgemont Village. She is the dentist, and I manage the clinic, so I know how quickly costs add up—and how frustrating it is when you need an answer from the District and cannot find the right person. I would give commercial applicants one contact at municipal hall and aim to provide an initial, coordinated response as quickly as possible. I would find out where permits get stuck, cut unnecessary red tape and allow sensible flexibility. When construction affects businesses, owners should know early and have a say on access, parking and deliveries. I would work with the North Vancouver Chamber to bring small business owners together in focus groups. I want to hear directly from them what is making it harder to operate and what changes would help. The District should communicate clearly and follow through. I would work to keep property tax increases as low and predictable as possible, seek senior government funding to ease pressure on local taxpayers, and consider targeted relief where affordable. Helping existing businesses expand, welcoming new investment, and building homes local workers can afford will help create jobs.

answers.name: Mike Little
answers.answer1: I will continue to support a new and improved bridge crossing the second narrows. As a Mayor's Council member, current TransLink Board Member, and the Co-Chair of the Joint Finance Committee of TransLink, I will continue to fight for TransLink supported public transit options to and across the North Shore including supporting the Bus Rapid Transit Program to get our buses out of congestion. I will continue to pressure major employers to either have a Public Transit incentive program for staff or participate in private shuttle service for workers coming to the North Shore.
answers.answer2: I have, and will continue to support shifting tax out of our commercial class to keep us in the bottom half of Municipalities for taxation. I will continue to use curbside regulations to support turnover in customer parking spaces. I will continue to support our Business Liaison program to have a direct line of communication between businesses and senior members of District Staff.

answers.name: Stephan Nieweler
answers.answer1: The North Shore transport crisis has local and regional causes, thus any minor spot improvements will not resolve larger structural issues in the network. I have conducted my own research while at SFU, and have clear evidence that a rail transit line is justified in the immediate term – not the long term. As a result, I have delivered a 3-point plan to unlock the North Shore’s gridlock within a decade: a) A new multi-modal bridge for freight rail (beneath), rail transit, HOV lanes and active modes (above) next to the Ironworkers’ Bridge (which has 30 years of life remaining); b) New HOV lanes extending from the Cassiar Tunnel to Taylor Way, facilitating a new express bus service across the upper North Shore from Horseshoe Bay to Phibbs; c) A rail transit line from Ambleside to Metrotown (SkyTrain), and downtown (via Hastings) with travel times beating the car (multi-level park &rides at Park Royal, Phibbs and PNE stations Businesses would benefit as staff and deliveries would finally be able to travel on an efficient, reliable transport network, with 25% of current traffic removed from the two inlet bridges.
answers.answer2: Small business needs three things from City Hall: speed, predictability, and a council that actually understands what it's like to run an enterprise. I do — I owned and operated a jazz club, pub and commercial building as I worked as a transport planner. I know how much a slow permit process or an unclear timeline can cost a small operator. As Mayor, I'll make local economic development a real priority, not a line item — pushing for faster, clearer approval processes so business owners aren't left guessing. I'll also keep growth and development policy predictable, so investment in our commercial areas isn't scared off by years of uncertainty. And I won't treat transportation and business growth as separate issues — they're the same issue. Gridlock delays deliveries, costs businesses customers and their workers time that they could be spending on the job. Unlocking our gridlock is economic development. Finally, affordability matters on both ends: businesses need affordable commercial space, and they need employees who can afford to live nearby. I'll keep housing affordability central to how we grow this community, because a strong local economy depends on people being able to stay here.

answers.name: Catherine Pope
answers.answer1: We need strong voices advocating to the Province and federal government for the infrastructure North Vancouver needs — including a new crossing with rapid transit - SkyTrain or LRT- and active transportation. Realistically, that will cost billions and take years. In the meantime, we need practical solutions. I will explore an east-west connector for local trips that bypasses Highway 1, push for more frequent and reliable transit, and safe, protected routes for walking, cycling, and scooters. This is also a business issue. Congestion makes it harder for employers to recruit and retain workers and for employees to get to work reliably. We need more workforce and missing-middle housing so people who work here can afford to live here, reducing daily commuting. I would also work with local businesses to explore employee transportation solutions, including east-west shuttles and incentives for employees who use transit or active transportation. Better transportation means a more connected community — and a stronger local economy.
answers.answer2: We need to cut red tape and make government a facilitator, not a barrier to business. That means faster, more predictable permitting, flexible zoning. A restaurant that successfully operated a patio during COVID should not have to start from scratch, pay for traffic studies and wait months for approval while losing summer customers. A doctor providing specialized therapy for neurodivergent children should be able to operate in an appropriate light-industrial space. And daycare regulations should recognize that a public park or playground next door can provide safe outdoor space. We also need to create places where people want to shop, stay and spend time. Walkable communities, town-centre plazas, farmers' markets, music and community events can bring people together and support local businesses. Finally, protecting employment land is critical to economic growth. I would explore pre-zoning appropriate areas for high-tech, clean-tech and green businesses, making it easier to attract investment and create good local jobs. The District should be working with small businesses — not making it harder to do business here.

answers.name: Daniel Anderson
answers.answer1: Transportation needs to be addressed at multiple levels. Vehicle traffic stems from a few central sources: our migrating workforce, including construction, retail and public sector, our ferry traffic and to a lesser extent our residents. If we intend to keep traffic moving, we must ensure we stagger flow onto our highways so the speed is maintained. That will require cross-municipality coordination. We also need to think practically about where and how to use laneage. For example, Mountain Highway needs another lane south that bypasses the bridge turnoff, while Keith needs to eliminate the parking on its southern edge to allow quicker turns onto Brooksbank. The province and federal government could also improve traffic by opening an earlier exit to Mountain Highway and providing funding for better highway infrastructure, including a new Ironworkers Bridge, which is nearing the end of its lifespan. Lastly, we need to ensure our transit is rapid, reliable and affordable– if it takes significantly longer to get somewhere by bus then people will elect to use their vehicles. This will require fighting for our fair share of transit investment on the North Shore and ensuring buses can bypass bridge traffic.
answers.answer2: The District must secure diverse, affordable commercial lease space for small businesses through targeted rezoning and by mandating appropriately zoned commercial units in new builds. It should also listen closely to business leaders about barriers to ongoing trade, whether they arise from permitting delays, traffic gridlock, or taxation. Property taxes are only one source of financial pressure on businesses. Employers are also facing eye‑watering levies arising from the mismanagement of the North Shore Wastewater Treatment Plant project, which has seen its budget balloon from roughly $700 million to $3.86 billion, with costs passed on to households and businesses via utility rates and special levies. Finally, the District should help employers retain reliable staff by supporting regional affordable housing and improving traffic flow so workers can reach sites on time. Effective small‑business policy requires pairing smart zoning with responsive regulation and practical transportation and housing solutions.

answers.name: Linda Munro
answers.answer1: There is no quick fix to transportation; greater collaboration and a multi-step approach is needed for change to occur. Transit: Long term, we need skytrain to North Vancouver. Short-term, we need more rapid bus routes, like the R2, because frequent bus service encourages people to take transit and gets cars off the road. I would like to see rapid bus service for routes that transverse North Vancouver such as the 210, 211, 232 and 240. Highway: Together with the Province, explore the possibility of an expressway lanes and collector lanes system on Hwy 1 across the North Shore. This separates through-traffic from local traffic to reduce congestion on busy multi-lane highways. Bridge: We need a replacement of the Iron Workers Memorial Bridge. The current bridge was designed in the 1950s for 1960s traffic levels. Cycling: Having cycling infrastructure increases road safety, which encourages people to go by bike and that gets more cars off the road.
answers.answer2: What I am hearing from small business owners is traffic, rising costs, tariffs and lack of support from the municipality is hampering the development of a vibrant business community in the District of North Vancouver. I want the District to be where people can live, work and thrive. Prioritizing maintaining and growing industry and commercial space so local residents can live and work in their community is important to me. Improving traffic will help local businesses. Additionally, I know that process delays hurt the bottomline of local businesses. I am interested in pursuing opportunities to streamline the permitting process to reduce delays and get businesses up and running faster. I would like to see clear communication from the District to local businesses if road work will affect streets around their business. Additionally, I will continue to listen to the voices of small business owners and work with Council colleagues to pursue changes that would encourage a diverse range of businesses that support the needs of local residents and strengthen our local economy.

answers.name: Lisa Muri
answers.answer1: We need a new bridge, IWM, expansion of the Port requires it, we can address some congestion with reallocating lanes and improving efficiency. We are beyond the point of improvement without big capital moves.
answers.answer2: Small business needs DNV support, faster permits, less bureaucracy, zoning to help attract, streamlined policy’s, reduced service fees, review of policies creating barriers negatively impacting small business.

answers.name: Mathew Bond
answers.answer1: The future of North Vancouver’s economy depends on our ability to move people, goods and services reliably across the North Shore. Congestion increases delivery costs, makes shifts harder to staff and separates employees from jobs. No single mega-project will solve this. North Shore municipalities, First Nations and businesses need to work with TransLink and the Province to advance rapid transit connecting Metrotown, the North Shore and Park Royal, while also improving the reliability of Highway 1 and the Ironworkers bridge. The District cannot promise a new bridge or control the highway, but it can present a united case for investment and coordinate local work. Locally, we need to do what is within our control. The District can provide transit priority, improve last-mile connections, and better coordinate construction and road work. More housing choices near employment centres and transit will also shorten commutes and expand the pool of workers who can reach North Vancouver businesses. I support quick and practical local improvements through pilot projects, where we can measure the effects on travel reliability, safety and business operations, and refine them. The goal is reliable access for workers, customers, goods and services.
answers.answer2: While the DNV’s business tax rates are competitive in the region, high commercial and light-industrial property values, provincial assessment rules and triple-net leases can create unexpected cost increases for businesses. The shortage of space for business activities, especially smaller light-industrial businesses, continues to push land values and lease rates higher. During my time on Council, I supported protecting and intensifying employment lands and zoning District-owned lands in Maplewood for a mix of light-industrial and artisan space and housing. I would continue advancing the Maplewood Plan to create more space for businesses, jobs and homes close to employment. As we create opportunities for new businesses to start and grow, I also support preventing non-employment uses from displacing businesses in the Lynn Creek and Pemberton areas. The District must follow through on its Economic Development Strategy by making permitting quicker, clearer and more predictable. I would continue to push for its implementation, with follow-up and monitoring reported to Council. I would also continue to support creating more housing and transportation choices in the District. Business owners and employees need a realistic chance to live near their work or get to work reliably.

answers.name: Stephanie Wilson
answers.answer1: I believe that we can’t just pave our way out of traffic congestion. My priority is public transit: building out a fast and reliable transit network to make it a real alternative to driving. Each person taking transit is one less car on the road contributing to congestion. Active mobility infrastructure is an important tool to keep people safe and provide another alternative to driving. It also helps people get to transit stops. Transit planning starts at the rider’s front door, not their bus stop. There are so many stops that don’t have sidewalk access, benches, or bus shelters. We need these improvements to make transit more accessible to more people. I do want to see a Skytrain to the North Shore, but realistically this will take many years. In the short- and medium-term, we need Rapidbus and Bus Rapid Transit. RapidBus service to Lynn Valley is in Translink’s plan. Two areas that I feel also need investment are east of the Ironworkers and on Capilano Road. I understand that it’s hard to buy into a plan when so many neighbourhoods have poor transit access. The R2 shows us what’s possible when we make good transit a priority.
answers.answer2: Build housing that workers can afford so that good workers stay on long-term rather than leave a job due to a soul-crushing commute. Help businesses retain workers by making North Vancouver a good place for workers to live. 3. Encourage reasonable home-based businesses and ground-floor commercial in new housing developments to help businesses bring their products and services where people already live. 4. Advocate for fairer commercial leases.

answers.name: Trey Bell
answers.answer1: I support an all-of-the-above approach to transportation: practical road improvements, better public transit, and safer, more connected options for walking and cycling. We cannot solve congestion by focusing on only one way of getting around. I would support having two southbound lanes on Mountain Highway approaching the highway to alleviate the Arborlynn bottleneck, expand community bus service, and work with TransLink and senior governments to improve transit and advance rapid transit, such as SkyTrain to North Vancouver, starting with connections to Phibbs Exchange and Capilano University. The District’s current financial plan already identifies rapid transit and improvements to the Highway 1 corridor and Second Narrows crossing as priorities requiring regional and senior-government partnerships. I also want to complete missing sidewalk and cycling connections, particularly in growing neighbourhoods where infrastructure has not kept pace with development. Most importantly, I believe future growth must be accompanied by the transportation infrastructure needed to support it. My goal if elected would be to provide residents more transportation choices while reducing congestion, and making it easier and safer to get around North Vancouver.
answers.answer2: Small businesses are vital to our local economy, and the District should make it easier to operate and grow a business in North Vancouver. Through my time working at Bee Haven Childcare, from a centre manager to a program director, I saw firsthand how a well run small business can grow, meet the needs of the community, employ local people, and create value far beyond its walls. I would work to streamline municipal permits and approvals, reduce unnecessary red tape, keep municipal taxes and fees reasonable, and engage directly with businesses before making decisions that affect them. I will not support introducing paid street parking in the District of North Vancouver. Access matters for customers, employees and local businesses. I also want to support vibrant town centres where residents can shop, work and access everyday services close to home. Future planning should ensure growing neighbourhoods have the commercial spaces, shops and services needed to become genuinely walkable communities. Transportation and housing are also economic issues. We should work with local employers to improve transportation connections and encourage diverse housing options so people who work in North Vancouver have a better opportunity to live here too.

answers.name: Victoria Nwabuisi
answers.answer1: My vision for transportation in North Vancouver is anxiety-free, reliable movement. I want every resident to feel confident getting up in the morning and heading wherever they need to go without worrying that a one-hour commute could turn into two. Now, this is the ideal! The reality is that transportation is complex. Provincial regulations, municipal responsibilities, TransLink and different levels of government can add layers of complexity to finding and implementing solutions. The Mayor and Council cannot fix congestion in a day. But this issue isn’t new, so what can we do? If elected, I am committed to listening—to residents who experience these challenges every day and to transportation experts who understand the system. I want to understand what is working, what isn’t, and what we haven’t tried yet. And throughout this process, residents need to be part of the conversation. We may not be able to eliminate congestion, but we can work toward a transportation system that is more predictable, practical and less stressful for everyone.
answers.answer2: When Columbus Farm Market closed permanently on June 30, 2025, I was so sad. After more than 30 years in our community, Columbus wasn’t just another retail tenant—it was part of the character of Edgemont. Our communities thrive when local businesses can afford to stay, grow and hire. If elected, I want to build on the work already underway and focus on making it easier to start, operate and grow a business in the District. That means listening to business owners, looking at municipal processes and permitting, protecting appropriate commercial and employment space, and understanding the pressures they are facing—from rising costs and commercial rents to parking, transportation and access to workers. Small businesses are the lifeblood of our community. I want to contribute to creating an environment where local businesses can put down roots, grow and continue to be part of the neighbourhoods we love.
